design_detail: Narrative, non-systematic review (the authors' own description) of human studies of sleep in people who use alcohol, cannabis, cocaine and opioids: self-reported and polysomnographic sleep during use, early abstinence and later abstinence, links between sleep and relapse, and medicines tried for sleep problems. PubMed, Ovid Medline and Web of Science searched with drug and sleep terms, plus reference lists; no dates, selection criteria or numbers of studies given. 222 references.
can_establish: What sleep changes the cited literature (up to about 2015) describes during and after regular use of each of the four drugs, as summarized by the authors, which medicines had been tried for those sleep problems, and the authors' framework linking slow-wave and REM sleep to relapse.
cannot_establish: How common or how large each sleep change is in people who use these drugs (no systematic selection, pooling or appraisal; most figures are single studies quoted without sample sizes); whether sleep problems cause relapse (the studies cited are associations); whether any sleep medicine helps in withdrawal (trials cited are few and not appraised); or anything about occasional use, since nearly all cited studies concern people with use disorders.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). Cited studies are mostly polysomnographic and questionnaire studies of people with alcohol, cannabis, cocaine or opioid use disorders in inpatient or outpatient treatment, compared with healthy sleepers or with their own baseline, and a few placebo-controlled medicine trials.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: None stated beyond the search terms; psychotherapy for sleep was deliberately left out.
sample.selection_effects: Selection by the authors. The cocaine section rests largely on studies from the senior author's laboratory (eight of 222 references, including Morgan et al. 2010 on modafinil); the opioid section draws heavily on methadone-maintenance samples; few studies of occasional use or of women are cited.

exposure.measurement: Varies across cited studies: diagnosed alcohol, cannabis, cocaine or opioid use disorder; laboratory administration in some acute studies; methadone or buprenorphine treatment.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as summarized: acute administration studies of THC (10, 20 or 30 mg) and of opioids; methadone maintenance (one cited study links doses above 120 mg a day to poorer sleep); trazodone 50 mg at night in methadone-maintained patients; amitriptyline against lorazepam in opioid withdrawal (amounts printed without units); buprenorphine and methadone tapered over two to three weeks in one study and buprenorphine tapers of one, two or four weeks in another. Abstinence periods studied range from the first night to several years.
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed systematically; one cited methadone-maintenance study found nicotine and benzodiazepine use associated with poorer sleep, and about half of methadone-maintained patients reported using illicit drugs or medicines to help sleep.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Central to the review: findings are organized by early abstinence (acute withdrawal) and late abstinence (subacute withdrawal), which the review does not define in days for all drugs.

comparison.controls: Healthy sleepers, or the same people at baseline or at other points of abstinence, in the cited studies; placebo in the cited medicine trials.
comparison.matching: Not described; the review notes that differences in how controls were recruited and matched for age may explain inconsistent REM findings in alcohol studies.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The review notes that sleep problems predict later substance use (described as bidirectional) and that depression shortens REM latency, both of which confound abstinence comparisons; premorbid sleep is rarely measured.

outcomes.instruments: Self-report (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, Epworth Sleepiness Scale, Leeds Sleep Evaluation Questionnaire, Sleep Disorders Questionnaire, Insomnia Severity Index); polysomnography (sleep latency, total sleep time, sleep efficiency, slow-wave sleep, REM sleep and latency, wake after sleep onset); actigraphy; sleep-disordered breathing measures.
outcomes.validity_norms: Not appraised. For cocaine the review argues that self-reports become unreliable in abstinence ('occult insomnia'), with polysomnography worsening while self-rated sleep improves.
outcomes.operationalization: Table 2 summarizes the direction of objective changes in early and late abstinence relative to healthy sleepers, with question marks for insufficient or conflicting data.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported for the cited studies.

analysis.effect_sizes: None pooled. Figures as cited: clinical insomnia in 35 to 70% of people with alcohol use disorder against about 15 to 30% in the general population; sleep difficulties in 32 to 76% of people in cannabis withdrawal, strange dreams lasting up to about six weeks in some studies; total sleep time around the third week of cocaine abstinence as low as 300 to 330 minutes, and slow-wave sleep at three weeks half that of age-matched healthy sleepers; more than three-quarters of methadone-maintained patients reporting sleep complaints; signs of central sleep apnoea in 30 to 90% of patients on long-term opioid therapy, in a dose-dependent way.
analysis.selective_reporting: Non-systematic selection; the authors' own cocaine studies are described in detail, while conflicting results in other sections are noted briefly (for example REM in alcohol use disorder).

interpretation_gap.results_show: As summarized, regular use of each of the four drugs is followed in abstinence by objectively poorer sleep (longer time to fall asleep, shorter sleep, less slow-wave sleep), lasting weeks to months and for alcohol sometimes years, with drug-specific patterns of REM change; alcohol and cannabis help falling asleep at first but lose this effect with regular use; self-reported sleep problems and some objective measures predict relapse in several studies; and the medicine trials cited give mixed or negative results for relapse even when sleep improves.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The conclusion speaks of overwhelming evidence of chronic sleep alterations common to all four drugs and proposes that medicines targeting slow-wave and REM sleep may be more useful than usual sleep medicines, which could be counterproductive. Gaps: (1) ‘overwhelming’ is asserted without a systematic search, counts or appraisal; (2) the relapse link is drawn from associations and offered as a mechanism; (3) modafinil is called the best present candidate for cocaine use disorder largely on the authors' own studies, while its effects on clinical outcome are described as mixed; (4) Table 2 marks most early-abstinence alcohol cells as insufficient or conflicting while the text describes clear changes. The review does label much of the mechanism as hypothesis.

timeline.event: Morgan et al. placebo-controlled study of modafinil and sleep in chronic cocaine use, from the senior author's laboratory and cited here as reference 147

replication.where_it_stands: A useful map of the sleep literature for four drugs up to about 2015, but not a systematic summary; figures should be taken from the primary studies it cites. Its cocaine section overlaps with Morgan et al. (2010), which another reader holds, and should not be counted as independent of it.

funding.funder: NCATS CTSA grant UL1 TR000142 (NIH) and the NIH Roadmap for Medical Research; NIDA DA-011744 (P. T. Morgan); Connecticut Department of Mental Health and Addiction Services.
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no competing interests.
funding.affiliations_note: All four authors at Yale. The senior author's laboratory produced several of the cocaine studies the review relies on.

what_would_settle_it: A systematic review with meta-analysis of polysomnographic studies in abstinence from each drug, appraising control matching (age, depression, other drugs) and reporting effect sizes by time since last use; and randomized trials of sleep treatments in early abstinence measuring both sleep and relapse.

domains.note: Databases are named but there are no dates, criteria or numbers; the authors call the review non-systematic.
No appraisal; findings are cited without sample sizes or designs in most places.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The cocaine section, including the recommendation of modafinil, rests largely on the senior author's laboratory; the other sections cite mainly other groups.
The slow-wave and REM framework for relapse and the medicine recommendations are presented partly as hypothesis and partly as conclusion.

domains.domain: Balance of sleep-promoting and sleep-disrupting effects across drugs
domains.note: Acute sleep-promoting effects of alcohol and cannabis, tolerance to them, and the benefit of opioids for pain-related sleep problems are reported alongside the harms.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No standard risk-of-bias instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3), so the editors' checklist is used; two domains are high, so the overall judgment is high. The review may be cited for its map of the sleep literature and as a second-hand source for the direction of sleep changes in abstinence, labelled as such; numbers should be taken from the cited primary studies, and it should not be cited for the size of any effect, for causation of relapse, or for the effectiveness of any sleep medicine.

key_findings.finding: The authors describe the paper as a narrative, non-systematic review of human clinical studies found in PubMed, Ovid Medline and Web of Science plus reference lists.

Alcohol, as summarized: alcohol shortens sleep latency in healthy people, but in alcohol use disorder sleep latency is prolonged during drinking and in acute and post-acute withdrawal, total sleep time is reduced, slow-wave sleep is deficient for months and possibly years, REM rebounds after stopping (with inconsistent findings), and sleep is fragmented from the second night of abstinence onwards; clinical insomnia is reported by 35 to 70% of people with alcohol use disorder against about 15 to 30% of the general population.
key_findings.locator: Alcohol › Subjective measurements; Objective measurements (Sleep latency, Total sleep time, Slow-wave sleep, Rapid eye movement, Objective sleep quality); Table 2

key_findings.finding: Alcohol, as summarized: self-reported insomnia and longer sleep latency in early abstinence predicted relapse in several studies, with mixed results for other objective measures.
key_findings.locator: Alcohol › Relationship between subjective measurements and clinical outcomes; Relationship between objective measurements and clinical outcomes

key_findings.finding: Medicines for sleep in alcohol use disorder, as summarized: gabapentin largely positive in trials; quetiapine improved wake after sleep onset and insomnia in one placebo-controlled trial with mixed effects on drinking; trazodone improved sleep measures but in a large placebo-controlled trial was associated with less abstinence during treatment and more drinking after it; ramelteon and agomelatine only in case series; benzodiazepines often avoided because of dependence and overdose risk with alcohol.
key_findings.locator: Alcohol › Pharmacotherapy options targeting sleep abnormalities, 1st to 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Cannabis, as summarized: short-term use eases falling asleep, but regular use brings tolerance; in withdrawal, sleep difficulties are reported by 32 to 76% of people, strange dreams typically start within days of stopping and can last weeks, and polysomnography shows longer time to fall asleep, more waking, less total and slow-wave sleep and REM rebound; returning to cannabis, alcohol or other sedatives to sleep is commonly observed.
key_findings.locator: Cannabis › Subjective measurements, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Objective measurements, 4th and 5th paragraphs; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Cannabis, as summarized: withdrawal sleep problems improve with oral THC or resumed cannabis use; zolpidem, mirtazapine, gabapentin and quetiapine improved some sleep measures, but none conclusively reduced relapse; valproate, lithium, nefazodone and bupropion showed no definite benefit.
key_findings.locator: Cannabis › Pharmacotherapy options targeting sleep abnormalities, 1st to 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Cocaine, as summarized: the first days to a week after stopping bring hypersomnia, bad dreams and fatigue; over the following weeks self-rated sleep improves while polysomnography worsens to insomnia-like levels (total sleep time around the third week as low as 300 to 330 minutes; slow-wave sleep at three weeks half that of age-matched healthy sleepers; low REM in weeks two and three), a pattern the authors call occult insomnia, linked to poorer sleep-dependent learning.
key_findings.locator: Cocaine › Subjective measurements, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Objective measurements (Total sleep time; Slow-wave sleep; Rem); Table 2

key_findings.finding: Opioids, as summarized: acute opioid use reduces REM and slow-wave sleep and increases waking; in the first week of abstinence from heroin total sleep time, slow-wave and REM sleep are reduced and sleep latency and waking increased compared with healthy sleepers, and in the first three weeks sleep latency is prolonged and efficiency reduced; after six weeks to six months of abstinence from methadone slow-wave and REM sleep rebound above baseline.
key_findings.locator: Opioids › Objective measurements, 1st and 4th paragraphs; Subjective measurements, 3rd paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Opioid treatment, as summarized: more than three-quarters of people in methadone maintenance report sleep complaints and about half use illicit drugs or medicines to help sleep; long-term opioid therapy is associated with central sleep apnoea (signs in 30 to 90% of patients, dose-dependent); buprenorphine treatment in 70 patients was associated with mild to severe sleep-disordered breathing.
key_findings.locator: Opioids › Opioids and sleep disordered breathing, 1st paragraph; Methadone, 1st paragraph; Buprenorphine, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Medicines for sleep in opioid withdrawal or treatment, as summarized: trazodone did not improve subjective or objective sleep in methadone-maintained patients; amitriptyline and lorazepam did not differ on most sleep measures in a randomized double-blind study of 27 people with withdrawal insomnia; methadone and electrostimulation were not effective for insomnia in withdrawal.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 marks all early-abstinence alcohol cells as insufficient or conflicting data, while the text states that sleep latency is prolonged and total sleep time reduced during acute withdrawal.
reporting_issues.consequence: The table and the text disagree; neither gives the underlying numbers.

reporting_issues.issue: The cannabis objective-measurements section refers to Table 1 (a glossary) for withdrawal changes that are summarized in Table 2.
The amounts of amitriptyline and lorazepam in the cited withdrawal-insomnia trial are printed without units.
reporting_issues.consequence: The study conditions cannot be read from the review.

reporting_issues.issue: The review uses stigmatizing labels rather than person-first language for people in the cited studies.
reporting_issues.consequence: Not an error in the evidence; quotations from the review need person-first rewording (METHODS §9).
